item.title: "The Man of Nobody": Re: "The Man of Nobody"
item.content:encoded:
It's an interesting coincidence that you came to me about this, because I wrote SCP-3550, which is very similar in concept. Let me warn you beforehand, this is my most controversial skip because humanoids are just difficult to do well, expecially because you have to make them (or supporting cast) interesting characters in order for it to be enjoyable, which is easier said than done. Some people like it, others hate it.

I think your best angle will be to focus on how or why he was cursed, since I placed much more emphasis on the interaction with Foundation personnel and we might want to differentiate the two somewhat. That doesn't mean that you don't put effort into the Foundation personnel interaction also, maybe just shift your main focus on how your skip ended up in this situation.

Finally, making humanoids is incredibly difficult as a first one, so there's no shame in shelving it for now and revisiting the concept when you have more experience.

item.title: The chamber of eternity: Re: The chamber of eternity
item.content:encoded:
Hi voidlocke, I'm still not too sure about this secondary effect:

If any instances of the person linked perceives any other instances of themself as superior, they become slowly more self-conscious, and then violent, attempting to take out the other versions, to become the "Supreme Version."

It sounds very much like a basic compulsion effect, i.e. instances forcing other instances to kill each other just for the sake of your plot. What's so special about the need to become this "Supreme Version"? is there a reason for this happening, and is there a link to the base anomaly itself (the Chamber)? Ultimately, I feel if you worked on this more, your central narrative might make better sense.

The ancient mage and council of kings angle is a nice historical artifact, but notice it doesn't go back far enough to explain the creation / purpose of the chamber to begin with, and how this compulsion effect first took shape.

item.title: "The Man of Nobody": Re: "The Man of Nobody"
item.content:encoded:
Summoned via PM:

Hi there Identity8866. Let’s take a look at your concept.

Overall, the concept was interesting at first, especially since you seem to be questioning the nature of human interactions and whether truly “No man is an island”.

Unfortunately, the concept falls apart rapidly due to plot inconsistencies or overcomplications that are not well explained. Why, for example, do people do when this happens? I believe it’s never explained / hinted at throughout your concept. Who placed this curse on him, and why?

Secondly, I don’t understand the nature of the anomaly. Okay, so they die “horrific” deaths, but how and why in those manners? You realise that a “horrific” death can be incredibly subjective, right? Some people would be terrified of dying alone, for example. More importantly, is there a reason why they die in such a manner?

Additionally, the concept itself is vague as “relationship” can mean pretty much anything? You mention “friend”, “enemy” and “loved one”, but isn’t an acquaintance also considered a relationship? Wouldn’t the Foundation agents who try and contain the man also be affected then?

Finally, I don’t understand that whole angle with suicide patients. How are they being “helped”?

Overall, there are too many plot issues for me to understand this fully. If you do decide to revise the concept / respond below, do drop me another PM and I’ll take another look. Best of luck!

item.title: (Seeking Greenlight) the Survivors: Re: (Seeking Greenlight) the Survivors
item.content:encoded:
Summoned via PM:

Hi there EnderDragon101. Let’s take a look at your concept.

Overall, I agree with Quadraginta’s assessment: the concept sounds too ambitious, with you including multiple anomalies with little to no explanation as to their purpose or intention.

Mind you, it’s not about whether the concept is heavily sci-fi or not. It’s what you do with the many elements you’ve cited. What does the GOC have to do shooting down an alien ship, for example? What does “Galactic.Co” have to do with the alien’s purpose for being on earth? Why cross a human with an orca to make the alien? Is it just to make them look/sound cool? Finally, the whole description of SCP-xxxx-2 and SCP-xxxx-3 is overly confusing. It’s not clear why you needed to have two different materials in the first place, and what their significance is to the Foundation or the GOC.

The danger of picking a sci-fi setting is most beginning authors feel that they can get away with including multiple out-of-this-world / bizarre concepts and then make the excuse that “Oh, it’s just because it’s sci-fi” for their existence. Sorry, but the base rules of storytelling still apply: tell us what’s happening in your Central Narrative segment, and ensure that all the elements are clearly linked together. A majority of your Central Narrative atm is simply describing the SCP, and not going into enough detail about the actual narrative.

I hope you continue working on the concept though. The strength of a sci-fi concept is that you can really think out of the box, but some restraint is needed here. If you decide to revise the concept / respond below, do drop me another PM and I’ll take another look. Best of luck!

item.title: (Still) Awaiting Greenlight / The Book of the Sinners: Re: (Still) Awaiting Greenlight / The Book of the Sinners
item.content:encoded:
About the first point:

Since this SCP is designed to "save humanity" from sinful volks within before the corruption is too advanced, it would make sense for the book to simply "force" a challenger. If it is really a bad idea, I could work out some sort of "punishment" or "bad thing" that would happen if within a certain time span no person chooses out of their own free will to take part in the trial.

About the second point:

I really intend to make the tests as impactful and individual as possible. So there is an individual trial for each person with no reoccurring tests from past participants. I plan to make it a big emotional arc with character growth.

Now the price at the end is a bit…I say even a mystery to myself because originally I planned to make a reference to SCP 001 "The Gate Guardian" but I am not sure if I am allowed to do so since I am a newbie and with SCP 001 being a big deal to make references to.

item.title: SCP - The Infinite Quarter: Re: SCP - The Infinite Quarter
item.content:encoded:
several change machines would be purchased by the foundations and placed in various laundry mats and arcades where agents disguised as workers will place the half the non anomalous coins in the change machines and gather the money for funding

I'm…not sure I follow this? Is the plan 'the foundation owns a bunch of change machines and uses them to convert the coins into notes' because uh,,,that's not how money works

Beyond this, my core issue is that 'the foundation tries to work out which coin is anomalous' feels…like it'd be really uninteresting as a follow up to the description since we already know that it's just, one coin being anomalous; but it also feels like the actual investigation might be just, really boring and a lot of repetitive 'we tested coins 1 through 100, none are anomalous' kinda things.

I feel like this needs a stronger central narrative that actually focusses on the like, coin duplicating and the Foundation using this for their benefit, and like, that going somewhere, whether it's like…just the Foundation gradually like destabilising the economy by printing money or like, the treasury department investigating them and trying to arrest folk for creating counterfeit currency or something.

item.title: [Seeking Greenlight] A sentient entity formed from a psychic virus: Re: [Seeking Greenlight] A sentient entity formed from a psychic virus
item.content:encoded:
hm. I kinda like the core of this: that the entity has this, collective intelligence and wish to better humanity, and it presenting increasingly extreme requests to the foundation who have to question how far they are willing to go to like…keep this thing satisfied.

My, concern is that it feels like it might be really hard to like, convey this conflict in an interesting manner: I guess really what I want to see is where the conflict goes and how the demands escalate? Like, to really get a feel for you having an idea of how you're going to pull this off.

The television show revival angle feels…like something that either needs to be the core conflict the article is built around or not included; having it as a minor thing would feel weird, I think. But I also think it'd feel…weirdly petty for the core so I'd probably not include it?

item.title: Looking for Greenlights | The Hapless Helper: Re: Looking for Greenlights | The Hapless Helper
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

SCP becomes pale and sickly if it cannot provide aid to others.

I'm a little hesitant about this, and this kind of thing in general: it's usually less interesting to me if you add anomalous properties to a SCP that force the Foundation to let it do things than if you have a good narrative reason for the Foundation to let it do things, y'know?

After intense review, the SCP was allowed to accompany scientists and help within the site it is located at.

I'm kinda hesitant about this because a large part of the idea here is that the SCP tries to be helpful and isn't?

I want to keep the focus of the article on the mysteries surrounding the SCP and its desire to connect with members of the Foundation.

What is this mystery? This feels like the it's meant to be the core of the article but it also don't particularly feel like something interesting to explore; but I don't really know how you're like…intending exploring this? Like, how are you setting this mystery up to the reader? How are you getting the reader invested in it's outcome? How are you resolving the mystery?

My concern is that it feels like the most interesting part of this is the bit between the SCP Allison joining the foundation and them discovering the Thumbling, and the thumbling growing into becoming an actually valuable member of the Foundation, and like, the story of their growth; and it feels like you've not really…covered that section at all?

item.title: Moonbug: Moonbug
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre (Optional): Sci-fi

Page Layout (Optional): Standard layout. Containment procedure, Description, addendums

Elevator Pitch: Object makes impact with moon and researchers at Lunar Area-32 find a parasitic lifeform with anomalous properties in the substance left by the object.

Central Narrative: A object collides with the moon not far from Lunar Area-32 and a team sets out to investigate it. At the impact site they find a crater with a dark substance from which they take samples and return to base. Further study of the substance shows that it contains a parasite that will enter the human body through a body opening or wound and attach to the brain stem. Once attached the host will experience anomalous effects.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: It's a quite simple story that I hope to make interesting through exploration of the SCP and it's effects, and possibly how it could be used to the foundations benefit,

Additional Notes:

item.title: LLUN Man Seeking Greenlight: Re: LLUN Man Seeking Greenlight
item.content:encoded:
It's what happens after the SCP foundation gets a hold of Twist that makes up what this article is about.

Okay but like…you vaguely hint at Twist answering questions and being involved in experiments, and there being this big mystery around the LLUN aura and I'm left just asking one question: what's the narrative purpose of this all? Where does it go? How are you getting a reader invested in this LLUN aura thing?

My concern is that once Twist gets captured, the interesting chase stuff falls to the wayside and is replaced by a vague mystery around a complex aura that both powers and hinders a dude with no real stakes to the mystery. It also feels like all the time travelling and looping stuff that sets this up falls to the wayside and is replaced by the mystery of a person who can know everything but can't convey it, and I feel like reframing that to be the core and removing the whole Jack angle might make this stronger?

Iunno, it feels like I don't really have a good picture of what you want to do here yet.

item.title: Good intentions: Good intentions
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Elevator Pitch: A semi-sentient liquid metal that bonds with a persons nervous system and tries to protect that person from harm, but ultimately does more harm than good.

Central Narrative: The SCP is an unknown liquid metal that enters a persons body through the skin, bonding with that persons nervous system. Whenever an object/person comes into contact with the skin of the host, the metal will rush through the persons nerves to the point of impact, surfacing out of the skin to form a shield that protects the person from physical trauma. The SCP accidentally damages the nerves when it travels through them, causing intense pain in the host in the short run, and loss of fine motor skills to loss of all feelings in limbs in the long run. Even if the SCP is inactive in the host, over time the host will develop symptoms similar to long-term mercury poisoning, which will result in death after 10-15 months.

+ show
- hide

The SCP will only have one host at a time, and will not transfer to another while the previous host still lives. It initially transfers by skin to skin contact with the previous hosts corpse, however if the SCP is without a host for an extended period of time, it will leave the previous hosts body and seek out the nearest human to bond with. If it is unable to find a host after leaving the previous host, it will become increasingly aggressive and stronger to break out and locate a new host.

Due to the SCP reacting to even the smallest contacts with the skin, it becomes nigh impossible for the host to complete small tasks, and even a small shift in their clothing can set of the SCP. Monitoring the effects the SCP has on its hosts is extremely difficult, because the SCP prevents the foundation from taking any samples while the host still lives, and most forms of scans are ineffective.

In order to contain the anomaly, the foundation will expose a D-class in a medically induced coma to the SCP, and try to keep them alive for as long as possible. After the death of the D-class, a new D-class will be put into a coma before transferring the SCP to them.


Hook/Attention-Grabber: Something created to protect humans ends up damaging them in the long run.

Additional Notes: Linked to the broken god.

item.title: A Photo Book of Murderers: Re: A Photo Book of Murderers
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

There is an eighty percent chance that within the first hour if the person whose photo is removed their personality will stop being overwritten however for every hour it decreases by twenty percent. And for every hour less and less of the subject's sanity is retained.

This feels … really video game-y? Like just the way it works makes it feel like it's a cursed item from a game and not like, a thing which exists? I think because of the like…rigid, one size fits all progression which feels like it's kinda glossing over how everyone reacts to stuff differently and so it'd affect different people to different intensities and with different recovery times.

Beyond this, my core issue with this idea is that at it's core, it's "thing what turns you insane", which is, generally not very interesting to me. The angle of tying this into the brutality of asylums isn't a bad idea here but it feels underutilised: it feels, almost more like something your pointing at to say 'wow isn't this horrifying' than like, something actually in the story that you're grappling with and showing the horror of?

It also feels like it doesn't go anywhere: there's no real arc or growth through this, so like, you might highlight the malpractice but you're not really telling a story with it so much as showing some material that is shocking? And it feels like this needs e.g. a single character or something progressing through this that builds up to some kinda ending that grants closure?

I don't think this idea is dead in the water so much as it feels like it needs to take all the pieces you've assembled so far and then use them to do something, y'know?

item.title: The Petrifying Statue: Re: The Petrifying Statue
item.content:encoded:
Hello, let me make some questions and suggestions here, bear in mind I am not an official critter, though :)

First of all I know it hurts to hear this but this is basically reverse SCP-173. It is a statue and it kills people in horrible fashion triggered by them looking at it. It isn't a bad idea per se but it feels very Series I and currently these kind of stories are not very popular so I think even if you made it into the main page you would get downvoted pretty hard.

Secondly, there is no narrative here, you are just explaining what the anomaly is. What is the arc, who are the characters, what is the purpose? Why should I care about this article and what should I feel and think of it?

Your idea has terrifying implications: what if the statues around us in parks and public spaces were petrified people? If so, are they conscious? Is it possible to revert this state? I think this is a concept you should explore.

Also, from personal experience, writing AWCY is harder than it seems. Not every art anomaly must be tied to them so if you want to pursue this aspect you should flesh it out, give it a clear purpose, explore the anartist's intentions and what message they are trying to pass. Make this a plot twist or turn of events instead of just a tag to your story: what if the petrified people were volunteer artists who wanted to become art themselves? What if the petrified statue is the anartist themself?

Lots of what ifs to explore and figure out but by the end of it you'll have a much more fleshed out article that will have a bigger chance to make it into the official list. Good luck!

item.title: (Still) Awaiting Greenlight / The Book of the Sinners: Re: (Still) Awaiting Greenlight / The Book of the Sinners
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

If no human voluntarily tests themselves within a day, the book will choose a sinful challenger within a certain radius around it.

This is generally a bad idea: forcing someone to use a scp is generally a lot less impactful than exploring what happens when someone chooses to use it.

Each of the two will give a unique perspective about the realm of the sins, the sins themselves (so to say their representatives), the seven tests, and the ones who failed the trial.

This feels like the meat of the article and my biggest issue is that I still don't have a good idea of what this is going to be like. Or, rather, my concern is that it feels very passive: there's no like, driving force here where we're invested in the outcome of this because there's no stakes to it? It doesn't really matter to use whether they succeed or not because it doesn't really change much. It could work without stakes if the actual tests are interesting, or with good characterisation of the researchers and like, a big emotional arc where they really grow over the course of the testing, but I'm not really sure what your plans are in regard to that?

You mention there's a prize if someone passes all the tests: this could be the thing that provides stakes but like, it really depends on what it is? If it's big enough, the Foundation might feel justified in throwing some d-class at this to try to get the prize, and that might get around the first issue I raised.
